content:
I was asked here:
https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/37631#issuecomment-4379102698
by @Floris van Doorn to discuss this PR on Zulip before I did any further work on it.

First of all: this PR was already split off from a larger version precisely because I felt there was too much content in that one. So while I am happy to split further (in particular most of the changes outside of the new file in the new one are about the Pi.prod -> Function.Prod rename, I believe) I don't know that splitting further is useful.

To address Floris's questions.

  • Why do we need both Function.Defs and Function.Init?
    It is a good question. We seem to use the Init prefix to refer to a file which could be upstreamed without issue to Batteries or core: my model for this was Mathlib.Data.Nat.Init. Honestly I suspect this is also mostly true of Defs but it seemed best to contain my new contributions to a new file, so that it was clearer for reviewers. We use Init.lean files in quite a few places but not universally.

  • Why do you introduce unscoped non-standard notation?
    My motivation for this PR initially was precisely adding this notation because I keep wanting it - fun x => (f x, g x) is a form that just occurs quite naturally quite often (I have encountered it in several unrelated contexts and it irritates me every time), and there's no way to compactly write it. So the answer is "I felt the notation was the point". Note that this PR does not, I think, add that notation anywhere outside this file: the only changes outside Init.lean are moving Function.dcomp and things to do with the Function.prod rename (which you have already indicated you would accept). Why is the notation non-standard: I did a good deal of research into the right notation to use, and was unable to find a universally accepted one for Function.prod that would also not be confused with an existing notation. The notation I introduce here for Function.diag is I think relatively standard: e.g. https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/diagonal+function.

  • fstComp and sndComp
    Yeah - they were a recent addition to the PR and I am still not sure about them for the reason you say. Originally I had this spelled using the composition operator: the issue is that it of course then needs to consider the dependent and non-dependent cases separately (∘' is not the same as ∘) and things looked a lot messier. Actually originally I just wanted to focus on the non-dependent case but recieved feedback that I should not neglect the existing Pi.prod. But I think the "XKCD 927" problem is a serious issue to consider. Essentially I just found fstComp and sndComp giving shorter lemmas that felt easier to use and I think easy to automate with, but I absolutely do think there's no point in unnecessary definitions so would be happy to strip them.

  • What is the purpose of e.g. exists_fstComp?
    In prior PRs I have often recieved criticism for not stating natural lemmas which arise: I may have been somewhat over-zealous here in adding them. exists_pair_prod is less useful if you also have fstComp and sndComp but I would argue it is nice to have a compact way of talking about the component of a map into a product.

  • Renaming Pi.prod -> Function.prod.
    I am happy to prepare a PR that does this alone.

  • I think the best way forward is to close this PR.
    I disagree I think - I think you are quite right that the rename should be a separate PR, but I am not sure how I would split this one further - I think it would be better to just base this PR dependently on the rename PR. I would otherwise be closing this just to open one with either the same content, or what we had agreed to keep.

I will say I object to the characterisation of this PR as doing "way too many unrelated things", and I do not think it is true that "many of these changes add new things to very basic files". As I say - all of the edits that add or change things to existing basic files are in service to the one part of the PR you have confirm you would like. So I am, I confess, confused about this criticism. If I had produced the PR I originally was working on - which added new definitions at the same time as putting them in lots of existing places - I think I would absolutely agreed - that would be an incorrect approach and that is why I originally abandoned it. But in creating Init.lean, in line with existing convention (I would have added to it had it existed), I was trying to keep my additions contained and focused.

On the other hand, and thinking self-critically, I think it could be true that this PR should not move Function.dcomp as it does, and it is probably unnecessary to add the lemmas it adds. If this is what you had in mind, I do accept that is an extravagance. I think that could probably be reverted, or moved to a separate PR, but as such I would prefer to then avoid using the dcomp symbol to allow for upstreaming. This is what motivated the fstComp/sndComp introduction, however.

I hope this message is the kind of constructive Zulip discussion you were asking me to initiate. Thank you for the feedback thus far.

I was a bit harsh because I thought you wanted this PR to be merged roughly as-is (without preceding Zulip discussion). Thank you for starting the discussion! (This stream might be less visited than the mathlib4 stream, though.)

I personally don't think we need to have notation for fun x => (f x, g x). I've used this map quite a bit, but usually with bundled maps (linear maps, continuous linear maps, etc.).
I could live with a scoped polymorphic notation that works for all these cases, but I don't feel a strong need for it, and I worry that it will hurt readability.
The regex fun [^↦=⟨(]* (↦|=>) \([^)], shows 200 hits in Mathlib, so this notation would be used decently often. If it also works for bundled maps, that number increases.

Natural lemmas about new definitions are good! I think that lemmas where the conclusion is an existential, even though you can explicitly construct a witness of that existential, are often not that useful.

I'd happy for others to weigh in on the notation introduced in this PR (if there are no/few comments here in a few days, maybe start a thread just with that issue in mathlib4).
The existential ones I included in that form because Function.Surjective is weirdly a Mathlib-only definition (I think).
Not anymore: lean4#10341 (edited to point to the correct PR)
I think at the very least Function.diag would be a good new definition to have - I do feel this.
That doesn't seem to be the case: docs#Function.Surjective. You might have to import that explicitly if you're very low in the Mathlib hierarchy.

Julia Markus Himmel said:

Not anymore: lean4#10431

Oh sick!!
When did this change?
Lean 4.24.0 was the first release with Function.Surjective in core
What are we on now?
It's possible I just missed this.
Mathlib is on 4.30.0-rc2 at the moment.
Anyway yes agreed no need for existential lemmas with that.
Wow, OK then!
Wikipedia has:
Screenshot_20260506-110556_Firefox.png
Can you comment on the choice ⋏ for the product function? It looks a lot like an exterior product, which it is not, so it's quite dangerous IMHO.
The only one of these existing notations I could see maybe working is the tensor product.
Would ×ˢ work?

Sébastien Gouëzel said:

Can you comment on the choice ⋏ for the product function? It looks a lot like an exterior product, which it is not, so it's quite dangerous IMHO.

I was looking for a symbol that visually represented "two maps coming together into one map" to me. I think in some ways the resemblance to the exterior product is not a coincidence. But it is hard to find something that won't be confusing.

I'm used to f×gf\times gf×g for Prod.map and (f,g)(f,g)(f,g) for Function.prod as mathematical notation. The first could work with an annotation, as Sébastien suggests. The second one seems pretty infeasible in Lean.
(unless we annotation one of the parentheses with a superscript?)
Maybe with f as the superscript rather than s? At least I associate that with the product of sets.
I do think that's a good idea though.
I don't know if you have any strong opinions about Function.diag notation.
I'm also not particularly sure the Function.prodMap I add is strictly necessary but it's there because it lets you do Prod.map with Function dot notation.
(Clearly you could also introduce dual definitions for the Sum where appropriate - indeed Sum.elim is already the nondependent version of that - but I decided that was a whole other can of worms.)
fstComp and sndComp perhaps aren't necessary at all. I think I currently have them as abbrevs and maybe that's enough. Again it's about adding dot notation as much as anything.
As you say the support for this stuff is pretty good in bundled maps (though I think Embeddings might lack them?)
Not sure it's helpful to start a new thread for it but #38963 captures just that rename, @Floris van Doorn
Oh - I remembered the other reason I couldn't use Function.Surjective: I think I was getting some universe issues. Maybe I can find another way to say it.
Got a stuck at solving universe constraint ?u.4873+1 =?= max u_1 (u_4+1) error.
Which I guess means one can't infer the universe that fits that equation, I guess because (u_1 - 1) is not a valid universe?
×ᶠ works well btw

Sébastien Gouëzel said:

Would ×ˢ work?

Isn't that notation for the product of sets?
Yeah, that is why I changed it to f rather than s.

Michael Rothgang said:

Isn't that notation for the product of sets?

Yes, but more importantly it's a typeclass notation, so designed to be reused in different contexts.
That's true, but for setlike things. I think you could argue that corresponding with SProd one could have an FProd typeclass

/-- A map into a product as a pair of components. -/
@[inline] def ofProd {ι} {α β : ι → Type*} (h : (i : ι) → α i × β i) : (∀ i, α i) ×' (∀ i, β i) :=
  ⟨(h ·|>.1), (h ·|>.2)⟩

@[inherit_doc] notation:max x:max "ᶠ" => ofProd x

This is a notation for "turning a map into a product into a pair of maps", which then removes any need to further define fstComp/sndComp, essentially bundling them together and giving access to a compact notation.

This would give statements of this form:

@[simp, grind! .] theorem fstComp_prod {f : ∀ i, α i} {g : ∀ i, β i} :
    (f ×ᶠ g)ᶠ.1 = f := by grind
@[simp, grind! .] theorem sndComp_prod {f : ∀ i, α i} {g : ∀ i, β i} :
    (f ×ᶠ g)ᶠ.2 = g := rfl
@[simp, grind! .] theorem fstComp_prod_sndComp {h : ∀ i, α i × β i} :
    hᶠ.1 ×ᶠ hᶠ.2 = h := rfl

The alternative notation would be to keep fstComp and sndComp definitions and use the notation:

@[inherit_doc] notation:max x:max "₍₁₎" => fstComp x
@[inherit_doc] notation:max x:max "₍₂₎" => sndComp x

That leads to statements like:

@[simp, grind! .] theorem fstComp_prod {f : ∀ i, α i} {g : ∀ i, β i} :
    (f ×ᶠ g)₍₁₎ = f := by grind
@[simp, grind! .] theorem sndComp_prod {f : ∀ i, α i} {g : ∀ i, β i} :
    (f ×ᶠ g)₍₂₎ = g := rfl
@[simp, grind! .] theorem fstComp_prod_sndComp {h : ∀ i, α i × β i} :
  h₍₁₎ ×ᶠ h₍₂₎ = h := rfl
I have moved this PR to draft and have begun splitting it into smaller pieces.
